source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Headline result. Across all 490 items in the founding studies, SP cut errors versus simple majority vote.
numbers: 490 items (Studies 1a-c capitals, 2 trivia, 3 dermatology, 4a,b art). SP cut errors 21.3% vs majority (P<0.0005, two-sided matched-pair sign test).
limits: Studies were not randomized, investigators not blinded, no sample-size planning, no preregistration. Gains differ widely by study (see b03, b04).
agent_relevance: The gain over majority is real but modest overall. Treat 21.3% as a pooled figure over friendly domains, not a guarantee.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Against confidence-based rivals, on the 290 items where confidence was measured, SP also won.
numbers: 290 items (Studies 1c, 2, 3). SP error reduction: 35.8% vs majority (P<0.001), 24.2% vs confidence-weighted vote (P=0.0107), 22.2% vs max-confidence (P<0.13, not significant).
limits: Max-confidence comparison was not significant. Majority is weaker on this subset than on all 490 items, so 35.8% is subset-specific.
agent_relevance: A self-confidence number is a weaker signal than a prediction about others when many are confidently wrong.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Effect size varied strongly by domain. Large on state capitals, small on trivia.
numbers: State capitals (Study 1a: 51 MBA students; 1b: 32 Princeton lab respondents; 1c: 33 MIT lab respondents; 50 items each): SP cut incorrect decisions by 48% vs majority. Study 2 (80 trivia items, 39 MTurk workers): only 14% error cut, P=.031.
limits: Capital questions were built so the famous big city is a tempting wrong answer. Not representative of natural questions.
agent_relevance: Gain depends on how often a confident majority is wrong. Biggest where a salient wrong answer exists.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Why Study 2 gave little: predictions were flat and the majority was rarely overturned.
numbers: In Study 2 the predicted vote splits fell in the 40-60% interval for 81% of items, versus 22% of items in other studies. This limited the chances for SP to change the majority.
limits: Only study using the MTurk pool. Authors do not prove why predictions were flat.
agent_relevance: If meta-predictions cluster near 50%, SP degenerates to majority. Check the spread of predictions before trusting SP.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Art study: majority is biased against the expensive category. SP lowers the needed vote threshold.
numbers: Studies 4a,b: 90 artworks, art professionals and laypeople. For a $100,000 artwork the average professional was right 30% of the time, yet the professional majority was right only 10%. SP cut the threshold for a high verdict from 50% to about 25%.
limits: Four price bins collapsed to a binary question around $30,000. Shows mechanism, not an overall gain.
agent_relevance: SP acts as a threshold shift for rare-but-true options. A rarely sampled candidate may be right if it beats its predicted share.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Dermatology study with professionals: gain exists but sample of experts is small.
numbers: Study 3: 80 skin lesion images, 25 dermatologists (mean 10.5 years experience; 12 saw 40 benign lesions, 13 saw 20 benign). Included in the 490-item pooled result.
limits: Per-study kappa values are only in the paper's Fig. 4 and were not extracted. Small N.
agent_relevance: Expert panels with shared training can still gain, which is the case SP is designed for.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Authors' own simulation: power to detect an SP advantage is poor with small panels.
numbers: Biased-coin model: individuals correct 75%, majority vote 86%. With 50 problems and n=30 respondents, SP superiority reaches P<0.05 in only 40% of simulated studies.
limits: Model assumes Bayesian respondents with a common prior and independent signals.
agent_relevance: With small panels (5 to 10 model samples) expect noisy results. Many questions are needed to test whether it helps.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Stated boundary conditions: SP cannot beat the information the respondents hold, and it needs honest predictions.
numbers: Requires a shared prior and conditionally independent signals given the true state. Authors state that if evidence is misleading, the answer fitting it may be wrong, and note manipulation risk; a BTS-like scoring rule can reward honesty.
limits: Assumptions are not tested directly; real respondents violate them.
agent_relevance: LLM samples from one model break independence and diversity (see b18, b22).
quote: SP performance will always be limited by the information available to the respondents and their competence.

source: Rutchick, Ross, Calvillo, Mesick (2020) Does the surprisingly popular method yield accurate crowdsourced predictions? Cognitive Research 5:57
finding: Preregistered NFL test (2018 season, up to 205 students): in the whole sample SP did worse than majority; with objectively assessed experts SP was narrowly best.
numbers: Total sample: individual 52.8%, majority 53.9%, confidence-weighted 55.6%, SP 51.4%. Objectively assessed experts (top quintile on a knowledge quiz, 46 people): individual 54.9%, majority 59.0%, confidence 59.7%, SP 60.2%. Media/algorithm benchmark fivethirtyeight 62.0%.
limits: Students, extra credit pay, no accuracy incentive; one season; differences are a few games.
agent_relevance: SP does not help when the crowd lacks real knowledge. Gating on real competence is needed.

source: Rutchick, Ross, Calvillo, Mesick (2020) Does the surprisingly popular method yield accurate crowdsourced predictions? Cognitive Research 5:57
finding: Preregistered 2018 US midterm test (110 races, 309 MTurk analysed of 401): all aggregators beat individuals, SP edge tiny, self-rated experts worse under SP.
numbers: Total sample: individual 60.8%, majority 79.1% (87/110), confidence-weighted 79.6%, SP 80.0%. Objectively assessed experts: majority 79.6%, confidence 80.0%, SP 82.7% (91/110). Self-assessed experts: majority 77.3%, SP 71.8%. fivethirtyeight 86.4% (95/110).
limits: Preregistered tests had very low sensitivity at n=110; authors moved inferential tests to the supplement. Self-rating of expertise is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Self-rated competence is a poor gate. A polling model beat every crowd method.

source: Rutchick, Ross, Calvillo, Mesick (2020) Does the surprisingly popular method yield accurate crowdsourced predictions? Cognitive Research 5:57
finding: NBA test (N=130, already knowledgeable fans): SP best crowd method by a small margin.
numbers: 465 games. Individual 61.8%, majority 65.9% (306.5 games), confidence-weighted 65.5%, SP 67.3% (313 games), fivethirtyeight 68.2% (317). Mean quiz score 12.6 of 19.
limits: SP minus majority is about 6.5 games of 465. No incentives. Authors call the overall pattern inconclusive.
agent_relevance: Where the crowd is knowledgeable, SP gives about +1.4 points over majority: small but same direction.
quote: our findings were inconclusive, although the SP method did yield the most accurate predictions when applied to the judgments of experts

source: Lee, Danileiko, Vi (2018) Testing the ability of the surprisingly popular method to predict NFL games, Judgment and Decision Making 13(4)
finding: Exploratory forecast test on 256 NFL games (2017-18) with 'extremely knowledgeable' MTurk participants (from 100 recruited). SP beat all comparators, by a small margin.
numbers: 256 games. SP beat AMT-expert mode, confidence-weighted tally, media-expert mode, Elo, and most of 94 individual media experts (who mostly got 155-175 right). Correlation between estimated and true agreement about 0.3 in most knowledge groups.
limits: Authors: results are exploratory and need replication. Self-rated expert subgroup chosen after looking at accuracy. Exact game counts only in Fig. 3. Rutchick 2020 (b09) did not reproduce it in the total sample.
agent_relevance: The best positive forecast result needed a post hoc expert filter. Beware forking paths.
quote: Our results are exploratory, and need replication, but we find that the surprisingly popular method outperforms all of these alternatives.

source: Martinie, Wilkening, Howe (2020) Using meta-predictions to identify experts in the crowd, PLOS ONE
finding: A rival use of meta-predictions: weight each person by how well they predict others (meta-probability weighting), instead of picking the SP option. It beat simple averaging.
numbers: N=459 MTurkers analysed (500 recruited, 41 excluded), 500 grade-school science true/false statements in 5 difficulty levels. Extremised MPW vs simple average +6.64 points [5.61, 7.63] on a 0-100 Brier-based score; vs mean individual +14.22. On the hardest level about 9 points over averaging. No significant gain at the easiest level; basketball dataset in the appendix showed no significant difference.
limits: One population and domain. Paper does not compare with majority or confidence weighting. Needs many items per person.
agent_relevance: Weighting by meta-prediction skill may be more robust than choosing the SP option on single items.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Shah, Shi (2021) Surprisingly popular voting recovers rankings, surprisingly! (IJCAI)
finding: SP extended to full rankings. Human study on geography, movies and artwork rankings: SP voting beat six classic voting rules.
numbers: 720 MTurk workers; 60 elections over three domains; six vote/prediction formats; over 82% passed the quiz. For top-of-4, random error is 0.75; individual votes and predictions each had error near this, yet SP combining the two was far lower. Rank-Rank SP beat Plurality, Runoff, Borda, Copeland, IRV and Maximin using one third of the samples.
limits: Error values are in figures only. Ground truth is numeric (population, gross, price). Same group later published b15 and b16.
agent_relevance: Two nearly useless signals (vote, prediction) can combine into a useful one.
quote: by combining these two pieces of individually erroneous information, SP voting is able to achieve significantly lower error

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Puhan (2024) The surprising effectiveness of SP voting with partial preferences
finding: Cheap partial elicitation (top-k or approval ballots) works. New MTurk study: Partial-SP and Aggregated-SP beat Borda, Copeland, Maximin, Schulze.
numbers: 432 MTurk participants; 3 domains (36 countries by population, 36 movies by gross, 36 paintings by auction price). Fitted proportion of experts under 20%. Partial-SP significantly beat Aggregated-SP; unordered approval ballots Approval(2)-Approval(2) already recovered ground truth well.
limits: Same research group as b14; numeric ground truths; figures only.
agent_relevance: Asking for top-k picks and a short prediction is enough. Full distributions are not needed.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Puhan (2024) Surprisingly popular voting for concentric rank-order models
finding: Theory: conditions under which SP-voting recovers the true ranking with high probability and how many samples that needs. Existing datasets show three groups (expert, intermediate, non-expert).
numbers: Concentric mixtures of Mallows and Plackett-Luce with G>=2 groups; 3 groups identified in earlier datasets. Exact bounds not read.
limits: Abstract page only was read.
agent_relevance: Recovery requires experts who are distinguishable from the crowd. Where all voters are the same model, there are no groups.

source: Han, Schoenebeck, Tao, Xia (2025) The art of two-round voting
finding: Two-round voting game with LLM voters. Round one is a public poll, round two decides; an SP-like strategy is an equilibrium. A reasoning model gains from seeing the poll, a non-reasoning model does not.
numbers: 40 agents (5 friendly, 3 unfriendly, 32 contingent), 50 votes per setting. Biased signal case (0.8, 0.6) informed-majority rate for DeepSeek R1: one-round 0.56 (accurate info) and 0.52 (vague); two-round 0.88 and 0.78. GPT-4o: one-round 0.50 and 0.52; two-round 0.48 and 0.50. Unbiased case: all 1.00.
limits: Role-play hiring scenario with stated prior and signal rates. Not a pure SP test.
agent_relevance: Showing earlier votes to a reasoning model lets it do an SP-style Bayesian update; a non-reasoning model did not use it.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025) Beyond majority voting: LLM aggregation by leveraging higher-order information (ICML 2026)
finding: Direct test of plain SP on LLM panels: SP is worse than majority vote. An inverted variant (ISP) and accuracy weighting beat majority.
numbers: Simulation, 4 agents with accuracy 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9. K=2 options: MV 85.13%, SP 79.94%, ISP 91.37%. K=4: MV 92.64, SP 90.52, ISP 94.94. K=10: MV 95.54, SP 94.40, ISP 96.81. Theorem 4.1: E[Adv_ISP] >= E[Adv_MV] >= E[Adv_SP] under their model.
limits: Second-order stats come from the LLMs' empirical answer co-occurrences, not from asking models to predict peers. Theory assumes agents beat random chance.
agent_relevance: For a panel of capable LLMs, do not pick the surprisingly popular answer. Majority beats SP.
quote: LLM agents are generally more powerful, so the systematic biases that SP exploits in human settings are much less pronounced here.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025) Beyond majority voting: LLM aggregation by leveraging higher-order information (ICML 2026)
finding: On real datasets the new second-order aggregators gain only 0.5 to 1.5 points over majority.
numbers: UltraFeedback, MMLU, ARMMAN (healthcare, K=2). Table 3 accuracy: 73.66 (OW) / 73.26 (ISP) vs MV 72.21; 90.37 vs MV 89.32 (OW), ISP 90.01; 85.78 vs MV 85.24. Single best model oracle: 73.14, 91.02, 85.32. t-statistics 12.53, 23.39, 3.22, all significant vs MV; OW beat MV in 97.92% of model-combination cases.
limits: Row-to-dataset order in the extracted table is ambiguous. Single best is a clairvoyant oracle. Panels of small open models (Qwen, Llama).
agent_relevance: Real gain from higher-order information is small; the cost of extra elicitation must be weighed against it.

source: Goel (2023, v2 2025) On the truthfulness of 'surprisingly likely' responses of large language models
finding: Token-probability SP for one model: choose the answer with the highest probability ratio relative to its prior (MaxRatio). Large gains on TruthfulQA for base models.
numbers: TruthfulQA 817 questions (437 adversarially filtered, 380 unfiltered). GPT-2 S/M/L/XL and LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B (4-bit). MaxRatio beat MaxPost by 16 points on GPT-2 XL and LLaMA-2 13B and 24 points on LLaMA-2 70B. Up to 70 points on single categories. Also tested on COPA and StoryCloze.
limits: Base models only; no chat or closed models. Binary-style scoring with 50% chance level. This is a prior correction similar to pointwise mutual information, not human-style meta-prediction.
agent_relevance: A cheap per-question trick for multiple-choice with logits: divide by the answer's prior.

source: Goel (2023, v2 2025) On the truthfulness of 'surprisingly likely' responses of large language models
finding: Where the LLM version helps or fails: robust to inverse scaling and quantization; helps most categories but not all.
numbers: LLaMA-2 7B: MaxRatio better in 28 of 38 categories, MaxPost better in 7, equal in 3. MaxDiff variant slightly reduced accuracy vs MaxPost. 4-bit quantization of 70B hurt MaxPost but not MaxRatio.
limits: Per-category samples are small, the author says the numbers get less conclusive. Variants (MaxDiff) fail.
agent_relevance: Prior-correction is not uniformly good; test per task before using.

source: Liu (2026) Bayesian truth serum for LLMs? (ICML 2026 workshop poster)
finding: Negative accuracy result: BTS-style scoring with LLM voters is about 1 point worse than majority vote, but improves calibration.
numbers: 871 code-review items, 4 LLM judges: every BTS variant about 1 point below majority, significant after McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. 150-item MMLU/TruthfulQA/ARC-C probe: same pattern. Expected calibration error down 21 to 32% vs majority. SP rule had lowest mean miscalibration.
limits: Poster abstract only, no arXiv version. Panel was saturated on the easy tier. Author withdrew the claim that the team beats the best single reviewer.
agent_relevance: Use SP-type scores as a confidence signal, not as the selection rule.
quote: Shared pretraining breaks the conditional independence assumption.

source: Luo, Liu (2019) Machine Truth Serum
finding: SP idea moved to classifier ensembles (heuristic and discriminative versions). Gains over majority are counted only on high-disagreement items and vary a lot between datasets.
numbers: 6 binary and 6 multiclass UCI datasets, 15 noisy classifiers (label flip rates 0.06 to 0.1). Heuristic MTS: 8 of 51 (+15.69%) Breast cancer, 48 of 149 (+32.21%) Spambase. Discriminative MTS: 70 of 76 (+92.11%) on one set, 1 of 64 (+1.56%) on Hill Valley.
limits: Gains counted among 8:7 to 9:6 splits only. Noise injected to make majority fail. Table columns mixed in extraction, so dataset-to-figure pairing is approximate.
agent_relevance: SP-like correction helps when a split vote is close; it is a tie-break tool for near-even panels.

source: Shinitzky, Shahar, Avraham et al. (2022) Exploiting meta-cognitive features for ML-based one-shot group-decision aggregation
finding: On hard puzzles, learned aggregation from confidence and predicted agreement beat majority, confidence rules and SP.
numbers: 2,490 responses to 22 problems; 77 random subsets of up to 30 responses; only 28% of respondents were correct. Learned RCR-Agg 64%, ACR-Agg 55%. McNemar tests: SP vs RCR-Agg p<0.0014; SP vs ACR-Agg p<0.0265; majority vs RCR-Agg p<0.00031. Abstract: +20% to 35% success versus rule-based methods.
limits: SP's own success rate appears only in a figure. The method needs training data from other problems.
agent_relevance: With a low solver rate, SP alone was not the best; a learned combination of metacognitive features did better.

source: Palley, Soll (2019) Extracting the wisdom of crowds when information is shared, Management Science 65(5)
finding: A competing fix called pivoting, which separates shared from private information. Cited by later SP work.
numbers: Not opened; only a search snippet seen. No numbers recorded.
limits: Unread. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Alternative if errors are correlated across samples.

source: Large Language Models Systematically Favor Popular Options (arXiv 2608.29257, EMNLP 2026)
finding: Not an SP test. LLMs choose popular wrong options; a prior-removal correction (PopDebias) restores accuracy. This is the reverse side of SP.
numbers: 22 open LLMs, 0.5B to 32B. When all distractors are more popular than the correct answer, models chose a popular wrong answer 66% of the time. PopDebias gained up to 54.1 points under strong popularity pressure.
limits: Abstract page only; the phrase 'surprisingly popular' is not used.
agent_relevance: Popularity bias inside one model is a concrete reason that majority over samples can be wrong, and a prior correction is plausible.
